sum: The Hang Seng Index jumped 2.9%, or 702 points, to 24,618 on Thursday, extending gains for a second consecutive session and reaching a five-week high.
The rally was primarily driven by improved global risk appetite following Democratic victories in the US midterm elections, which fueled hopes of renewed efforts to end the Middle East conflict.
Brent crude plunged more than 8% to below US$95 per barrel, easing inflation concerns, while lower US Treasury yields and a weaker dollar.
Buying interest was further boosted by Wall Street’s strong rebound, with the S&P 500 rising 1.6% on Wednesday, its biggest advance in three months, while the Nasdaq 100 gained 0.9%.

Domestically, Beijing’s market-stabilization efforts reinforced sentiment, as state-backed funds directed around US$11.5 billion into nine ETFs, while applications for PBOC-backed share-buyback loans exceeded CNY200 billion.
Top gainers were Tencent (4.9%), Xiaomi (4.0%), Meituan (5.6%), Alibaba (2.6%), and AIA (2.4%).

sum: Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 0.42% to 23,393.32 on Monday 2 November 2026, its second straight gain, as the Hang Seng Tech Index surged 2.25% led by Xiaomi, CATL, Alibaba and Tencent, while banks and gold miners lagged.

The Hang Seng Index, the main benchmark of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, closed at 23,393.32 on Monday, up 98.90 points or 0.42%, according to Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing data reported by Xinhua and The Standard. It followed Friday's 1.5% rebound and marked the index's first session of November in positive territory.

The index traded as high as 23,543.30 but gave back part of those gains in the afternoon. The more significant move came in technology: the Hang Seng Tech Index jumped 2.25% to 3,839.41 after rising as much as 3% intraday, while the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index added 0.56% to 7,906.11. Full-day turnover reached HK$204.84 billion.

Two forces supported the market. First, expectations of fresh policy support in mainland China lifted sentiment, after regulators met banks and brokers to discuss stabilising the equity market and the People's Bank of China signalled a new liquidity operation. Chinese brokerage stocks were among the leaders as investors bet on higher trading volumes.

Second, easing oil prices and a recovery in US stock futures after Friday's technology sell-off gave investors confidence to buy back into beaten-down tech names ahead of Apple's quarterly results. Even so, the gain in the broader Hang Seng was modest because banks and gold-related stocks, which had served as havens in October, were sold to fund purchases elsewhere.

Xiaomi was the best-performing blue chip, rising 6.1%, followed closely by battery giant CATL, which gained about 6% as lithium battery shares rallied. Among the heavyweights, Alibaba climbed 2.5% and Tencent advanced 2.2%, together providing a large share of the index's points gain.

Chipmakers also recovered. Hua Hong Semiconductor rose nearly 3% and SMIC added 1.5%. Casino operators climbed despite a decline in Macao's October gaming revenue, with Galaxy Entertainment up 3.7% and Sands China up 3.1%. On the downside, Bank of China and BOC Hong Kong were among the weakest constituents after their recent results, and gold miners eased.

sum: Hong Kong stocks traded choppily and weakened on the 29th. The Hang Seng Index rose about 90 points in early trading before selling pressure emerged, with losses widening to nearly 170 points in late trading as the 23,000 round-number level was breached again. The index ended at 22,958.65, down 136.18 points or 0.59%, with the daily candlestick turning black. The Hang Seng Tech Index fell more sharply, closing at 3,744.14, down 109.58 points or 2.84%. Main board turnover exceeded HK$189.4 billion (approximately $24.1 billion).

The correction was centered on AI and semiconductor names. Rising doubts over whether massive AI capital spending can translate into actual returns weighed on related stocks. Lenovo Group plunged 6.9% in a single session, while MINIMAX, Zhipu and Tianshu Zhixin fell 7% to 9%. Chip stocks weakened in tandem, with SMIC down nearly 6% and Hua Hong Semiconductor down more than 7%, as optical communications, memory and chip-related concept stocks came under broad pressure.

Large internet stocks were also not spared from the adjustment, with JD.com, Tencent, Meituan and Alibaba falling between nearly 2% and nearly 3%. Kuaishou and Bilibili pulled back noticeably, while Xiaomi edged higher against the trend.

Notably, capital clearly rotated out of technology names into financial and energy sectors. Ping An Insurance and PetroChina both rose nearly 3% after reporting earnings, while Chinese bank stocks advanced against the market, with the four major state-owned banks and China Merchants Bank gaining between more than 1% and more than 2%, becoming a supporting force for the broader market.

In contrast to the prior session, the Hang Seng Index had just closed up 0.23% on the 28th, and the Hang Seng Tech Index had surged 1.4%, led by storage, semiconductor and optical communications sectors. Hua Hong Semiconductor jumped more than 8% that day, and Lenovo Group also climbed more than 6%. In just one trading day, market sentiment shifted from optimism to caution, indicating that the valuation of the AI theme has entered a highly sensitive and volatile phase.

sum: Tencent, Alibaba and Hengke pull back: the market starts to price AI investments based on returns

On October 22, the Hang Seng Tech Index fell 5.03% to close at 3793.93 points. The index's trading volume reached HK$72.599 billion, up 55.9% from HK$46.56 billion in the previous trading day, marking the highest single-day level since October.
Tencent Holdings (0700.HK) fell 2.89% to close at HK$382.40; Alibaba (09988.HK) dropped 6.12% to close at HK$97.35, falling below the HK$100 threshold.

Just two days ago, the Hang Seng Tech Index was still above the 4000-point mark. Calculated from the intraday high of 6715.46 points on October 2, 2025, the Hang Seng Tech Index has retraced 43.5%. Since the beginning of this year, the Hang Seng Tech Index has fallen 31.2%, Tencent has dropped 35.4%, and Alibaba has decreased 31.2%.

In terms of capital flows, in August, Alibaba placed new shares to raise approximately HK$80 billion, which will be invested in AI capabilities and infrastructure. Tencent announced a new round of USD and RMB bond issuances in October — both companies are expanding their AI investment, however, the market has begun to "press for answers" on how previous investments can be converted into cash flow and profits at a faster pace.

At the macro level, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note remains above 5%, and the scale of Hong Kong IPO financing has also increased significantly since the start of this year. Interest rates, corporate expenditures and stock supply are jointly changing the price that buyers are willing to pay.

The share price adjustments of Tencent and Alibaba reflect that the market has begun to recalculate the returns on AI investments. In the past, increasing investment in computing power and models was enough to support growth expectations; now, investors are more concerned about how much revenue, profit and per-share cash return new investments can bring. The Hang Seng Tech Index has fallen in tandem, and this return verification has expanded from the two companies to the entire sector.

sum: Hong Kong equities returned from Monday's Chung Yeung Festival holiday with a broad decline on Tuesday 20 October 2026, as the Hang Seng absorbed two days of global news, the unchanged Chinese lending rates and a fresh sell-off in technology shares.

The Hang Seng Index closed at 23,867.74 points on Tuesday 20 October 2026, down 319.09 points or 1.32% from Friday's close of 24,186.83, according to Xinhua and RTHK data. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index fell 1.21% to 8,030.26, while the Hang Seng Tech Index dropped 1.52% to 4,045.91.

Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing kept its securities markets closed on Monday 19 October for the day following the Chung Yeung Festival, which fell on a Sunday this year. Tuesday's session was therefore the first chance for Hong Kong investors to react to China's third-quarter GDP data, Monday's rebound in US technology stocks and the People's Bank of China's loan prime rate decision.

The Hang Seng finished at 23,867.74, a loss of 1.32%, wiping out Friday's 0.52% gain. The index stayed in negative territory throughout the session, with selling pressure intensifying in the afternoon and no meaningful recovery into the close.

The close leaves the benchmark back below the psychologically important 24,000 mark. Reuters reported that the Hang Seng Tech Index touched a two-year low during the session, underlining the scale of the pressure on Hong Kong's technology sector.

Technology and financial stocks led the decline after China left its key lending rates unchanged, according to RTHK. The one-year loan prime rate stayed at 3.00% and the five-year rate at 3.50%, the 17th consecutive month without a change. Stronger-than-expected growth reduced hopes that Beijing would deliver additional stimulus.

China's economy grew 4.5% year on year in the third quarter, accelerating from 4.3% and beating the 4.4% consensus, driven largely by exports. Good news for the economy turned into bad news for markets that had been hoping for easier monetary policy. Regional weakness compounded the move, as Japan's Nikkei fell 1.30% and South Korea's KOSPI slumped 3.73% on concerns about AI spending and rising bond yields.

sum: The Hang Seng Index dropped 251.04 points to 24,510.09, its third straight decline, after touching a two-month low at midday as Chinese technology stocks slid and investors found little substance in the Trump-Xi summit. Mainland markets were closed for the Mid-Autumn Festival.

The Hang Seng Index closed at 24,510.09 on Friday, 25 September 2026, down 251.04 points or 1.01% from Thursday's close of 24,761.13, according to Google Finance and ME News data. The index opened at 24,523.50, already well below the previous close, reached a high of just 24,537.14, and slid to an intraday low of 24,275.56 during the morning session.

At the midday break, Reuters reported the index down 1.7% at 24,343.19, its lowest level in two months. The afternoon brought a partial recovery of more than 230 points from the low, but the benchmark still finished firmly in the red. It was the third consecutive losing session, following a 1.01% drop on Wednesday and a 0.29% decline on Thursday, and it leaves the index about 2.3% below its 22 September close of 25,087.75.

Technology shares led the declines. The Hang Seng Tech Index fell 1.13% to 4,311.78 at the close, after dropping more than 2% to a three-month low in the morning, with NetEase, Xiaomi and AAC Technologies among the notable losers, down between 1.8% and 3.05%, according to ME News. Reuters reported that AI-related stocks slid nearly 3% at one point, and the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index, which tracks mainland companies listed in the city, fell roughly 2% in the morning.

The macro trigger was the global bond sell-off. On Thursday, the US 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.225%, its highest since 2007, while the 30-year hit its highest since 2004. Higher US yields tend to pressure Hong Kong particularly hard because the city's currency peg ties local interest rates to US policy and because growth-oriented Chinese technology stocks are sensitive to the discount rate applied to future earnings.

Investors had hoped the Washington summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping would deliver a clearer framework for trade relations. Instead, Reuters described the meeting as heavy on symbolism but without apparent breakthroughs on AI, trade, Taiwan or the Iran conflict.

sum: Hong Kong stocks suffered a heavy blow on the first trading day of October, with the Hang Seng Index losing the psychologically important 24,000-point level and posting its steepest single-day decline in nearly half a year. On October 2, the benchmark index traded in a narrow range at low levels throughout the day, with intraday losses widening to as much as 3% before closing at 23,972.29, down 640.98 points or 2.6%—the largest single-day drop since the 3.54% decline on March 23. The Hang Seng Tech Index weakened in tandem, closing down 2.26% at 4,157.94, while the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index fell 2.31% to 8,030.54.

From a sector perspective, physical AI concepts, real estate, new energy vehicles, pharmaceuticals, and financials bore the brunt of selling pressure, while the optical communications supply chain bucked the trend and memory chip-related products also delivered notable gains.

The external pressure behind Hong Kong's sharp decline stemmed from a chain reaction in global bond markets. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since 2002, while the 30-year yield hit a 24-year high. The UK 30-year gilt yield briefly breached 6% for the first time since 1998, and Japan's 10-year government bond yield had already risen above 3% in September—the highest since 1996—demonstrating that the rise in long-end rates is not unique to the United States. Elevated long-end yields push up financing costs for financial institutions and compress asset valuations, making this the core drag on the day's trading.

A vacuum in capital flows amplified the decline. The Stock Connect southbound channel was suspended from October 1 due to the mainland China National Day holiday and will not resume until October 8. Mainland A-shares are also closed through October 7. With southbound capital absent, Hong Kong stocks lost a crucial source of incremental buying.

Pressured by surging long-end rates, international financial stocks were among the day's worst performers. AIA Group (1299.HK) fell 5.98% to HK$69.2 (approximately $8.8), hitting a near one-year low and ranking as the worst-performing blue chip of the day.

sum: The first half of 2026 saw Hong Kong stocks continue to face pressure amid a global market polarized between "AI and non-AI" plays. CICC's latest research report argues that the weakness in Hong Kong stocks is not accidental but a direct reflection of the "weaker consumption side of the K-shaped economy," further compounded by a structural mismatch in the tech sector and a "tight balance" caused by constrained liquidity. As of press time, the Hong Kong market has been in a downtrend for nearly nine months since early October last year, with the pullback exceeding 30%, and the internet sector plunging more than 40%.

CICC further points out that the current state of Hong Kong stocks is more of an "intermittent low" rather than a "major bottom" in the historical sense. Judging by the magnitude of the correction and valuations, the Hang Seng Tech Index has pulled back significantly, with some heavyweight stocks' valuations nearing extremes. However, from the perspective of earnings "capitulation," capital flows, and sentiment structure, the market still lacks a "policy bottom" catalyst of the same force seen at historical pivotal lows. The report provides a base-case judgment: if earnings grow 3%-4% and US Treasury yields edge lower, the Hang Seng Index (HSI) central range would be between 26,000 and 27,000 points, remaining largely range-bound, with upside dependent on a policy pivot.
Why Hong Kong Stocks Are Weak: Credit Cycle Turns Soft, Compounded by Structural Mismatch

CICC believes that the performance of Hong Kong stocks in 2026 is highly correlated with the global market's "tech theme," but the index composition of the Hong Kong market dictates a higher sensitivity to macro consumption. The report notes that the composition of Hong Kong's benchmark indices is closely tied to China's overall consumption, and this holds true even for the Hang Seng Tech Index: internet, e-commerce, new energy vehicles (NEVs), and new consumption sectors collectively account for over 70%, while the weighting of AI-related hardware tech is relatively small. Even though large model companies and some A-to-H share conversion companies have recently been included in the index, they remain at low weightings and were added relatively late.
